title: Trump defers federal diesel taxes to help farmers, but states issue warnings
description: President Trump's executive order deferring federal taxes on diesel is aimed at helping farmers but it's more complicated than it sounds and st
body:
President Trump's executive order deferring federal taxes on diesel is aimed at helping farmers but it's more complicated than it sounds and states are warning drivers they may owe taxes later.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  President Trump signed an executive order at a campaign rally in Nebraska earlier this month designed to appeal to rural voters - making diesel cheaper. But, turns out, it's not so simple, and it's causing a lot of confusion, as South Dakota Public Broadcasting's Jackson Dircks explains.(SOUNDBITE OF TRUCK IDLING)JACKSON DIRCKS, BYLINE: At a farm co-op in Salem, South Dakota, population 1,300, Gerald Otte is topping off his big, white 18-wheeler full of soybeans. It burns diesel.(SOUNDBITE OF TRUCK RUNNING)GERALD OTTE: It's a lot. I mean, it's $2.50 that we're paying more. You know, we were at 3.50, and now we're at 5.89. It's a lot.DIRCKS: This gas station is in farm country. So Otte can choose between two kinds of diesel. One dyed red is 24.4 cents a gallon cheaper. That's because it's exempt from federal highway taxes. It's the same as regular diesel, except for its color. It can only legally be used off-road, like in tractors. Trump's executive order says it's now OK to fill up highway vehicles with red diesel through the end of the year.(SOUNDBITE OF TRUCK RUNNING)OTTE: I think that pickup just did.DIRCKS: But Otte says his company told him to keep using regular non-dyed diesel.OTTE: They said I shouldn't do it because they're probably going to end up coming back and taxing us on that red fuel eventually.DIRCKS: That's because...MOLLY NIXON: The president really doesn't have the legal authority to say to the IRS, don't collect the tax. Don't assess the tax.DIRCKS: Molly Nixon is a senior fellow in executive power at the Cato Institute, a libertarian-leaning think tank. Trump's order only defers payment of federal taxes. So companies like Otte's are worried if they buy the red, untaxed diesel now, they're going to get a bill for it later.NIXON: So there's sort of a recognition here that actually getting rid of the tax might take more than any agency can do at this point - might require legislation.DIRCKS: South Dakota's governor is also telling people not to fill up their highway vehicles on dyed diesel. He's a Republican Trump fan who's up for reelection in a very pro-Trump state. But...LARRY RHODEN: At the end of the day, when the dust settles, we're going to take our time and make sure that nobody's caught in the backwash of unintended consequences because it is very confusing.DIRCKS: And just like Trump is telling the IRS not to penalize people for using dyed diesel, Rhoden's directing state officials not to check gas tanks for it throughout the year. State Democrats, though, want Rhoden to call a special session to suspend the state's 28 cents per gallon diesel tax. South Dakota's state's Trucking Association sent out a flyer advising not to change fuel practices because of the uncertainty about potential tax liability.Back at the co-op in Salem, Scott fills up a big diesel truck he's driving to a grain mill. He's not using the cheaper, red-dyed diesel either.SCOTT: Yeah. I heard so - that Trump OK'd it, but I don't know if I totally trust on that, you know, unless they gave you a piece of paper.DIRCKS: Scott requested we only use his first name because he said he's had negative experiences after being interviewed by the media and is concerned about his reputation in a small town. Trump has won this county by close to 70% in the last three elections, but Scott is frustrated.SCOTT: I think it's asinine when you got to pay over a thousand dollars to fill your truck up. Yeah, I remember that happening a few years ago, but this is just ridiculous, I think.DIRCKS: On Wednesday, the IRS said it won't inspect vehicles or impose penalties on people using cheaper dyed diesel on highways for the rest of the year. It says it, quote, "anticipates that it will offer further guidance" about postponing the tax and "explore avenues to eliminate" the requirement to pay it. For NPR News, I'm Jackson Dircks in Salem, South Dakota.(SOUNDBITE OF OSMAN'S "LOOK AT THE SKY")

title: Greensboro, NC students protest the absence of early voting sites on campus
description: NPR's Ayesha Rascoe talks to North Carolina A&T student Shia Rozier about disappointment with early voting sites in Greensboro.
body:
NPR's Ayesha Rascoe talks to North Carolina A&T student Shia Rozier about disappointment with early voting sites in Greensboro.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  Election Day is just a couple of weeks away, but in many states, early voting is already underway. In Greensboro, North Carolina, hundreds of college students marched to the polls on Thursday last week, the first day of early voting there.UNIDENTIFIED PROTESTERS: Democracy looks like.UNIDENTIFIED PROTESTER: This is what democracy looks like.UNIDENTIFIED PROTESTERS: This is what democracy looks like.RASCOE: They were protesting the fact that there are no on-campus early voting sites at two large schools, UNC Greensboro and North Carolina A&T University, the largest HBCU in the country. Shia Rozier is a senior at North Carolina A&T. She's also the co-founder of Protect Ours NC, a student organization seeking to make voting more accessible for North Carolina students. Shia, thank you for being with us.SHIA ROZIER: Thank you for having me.RASCOE: Why was it upsetting or a problem for students that there aren't early voting sites on campus? Like, it sounds like you were able to march to a voting site. So why was this a protest for you guys?ROZIER: Yeah, I think it kind of comes down to two things. One, what accessibility truly means for college students. You know, North Carolina A&T, the largest HBCU, just our last incoming class with over 3,500 students. But of those students, you know, there's a policy that students can't have their car within their first year. So all of them are essentially landlocked onto campus, meaning that in order to get to the polls, they now have to get a Lyft or get a Uber or get somebody to take them at a time where gas prices are extremely high, creating an additional barrier to the poll.And then also another problem that we have is that, you know, it's not really a resources issue because this year we saw our local board of elections grant another polling site to an area that had not been protesting and asking for months and months on end for a polling site. So it just demonstrated that they can give resources and polling site to the places that they want, but it just isn't at North Carolina A&T or UNCG.RASCOE: Well, what was the march to the polls like? I mean, Greensboro is not known for being, like, a walking city.ROZIER: Definitely not. That was a march that was organized by our A&T chapter Dems. And, you know, I think it was just to demonstrate that, you know, despite the board of elections' decisions, that they wouldn't be able to deter us from going to vote. Polling site or not, we're going to go and vote. Greensboro definitely is not a walkable city. It was over a 45-minute walk across train tracks, and it was even more inaccessible than the last polling site that we had away from campus. And I think we're just getting further and further from what true democracy looks like.RASCOE: Have there been early voting sites on campus in previous elections? And was there any explanation for why there weren't any there this year?ROZIER: Yeah, so as we look to early polling sites at North Carolina A&T, for the presidential election we certainly had one. And I think, you know, you'll hear from our board of elections that we've never had one in a midterm election. And, you know, I think it was a problem then, and it's a problem now. And what we've been saying is that, you know, the past mistakes shouldn't set the precedent for the present, especially when we're asked for something different. We are using voting planned sites from 2022 to determine what accessibility looks like for the class of 2030, and that's a real problem. Different times call for different measures. And as representatives, it's their duty to listen to their constituents and what they're coming to them with now.If we look at what it is that they've been saying - it fluctuates depending on the day, whether it's parking, whether it's, you know, the location - however, anytime that we've reached out to them to have one-on-one meetings to address any of their concerns and, you know, be able to remediate them, the people who have voted against our polling site have not reached out. So I think these are things that they're not looking to remediate. They just don't want to give us a polling site.RASCOE: Do you know, like, if this voting issue has been an issue at other colleges and universities? Like, not having polling sites on campus?ROZIER: Indeed, and it's fluctuated. I know that for the primaries, Western Carolina had their polling site taken away. I know at NC State now, theirs has been removed from their student union to a more inaccessible portion of their campus. Elizabeth City State is facing other issues like this. And I'm sure there's other ones that are facing this, not just in North Carolina, but throughout the nation. So I think right now we are all at a crossroads where we are deciding to stand up for what is ours and, you know, demand what we need and then also begin to build what we deserve.RASCOE: That's Shia Rozier. She's a senior at North Carolina A&T studying public relations. Thank you so much for joining us.ROZIER: Thank you again for having me.

title: Week in Politics: Trump's Russian diesel deal update; why the DOJ is suing California
description: Week in Politics: Trump’s Russian diesel deal update; why the DOJ is suing California
body:
Week in Politics: Trump’s Russian diesel deal update; why the DOJ is suing California
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5998079/nx-s1-9967961" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      We look at where things are in the deal President Trump says he made to import Russian diesel, plus the reason why the Justice Department is suing California.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  President Trump last night signed an executive order that waived sweeping sanctions against Russia. This follows last week's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel. Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries this week, following Russian strikes on Ukrainian power plants. These attacks came just a few days after President Trump announced the deal, which was to include an energy ceasefire. NPR's Ron Elving joins us. Ron, thanks for being with us.RON ELVING, BYLINE: Good to be with you, Scott.SIMON: President Trump blames high fuel prices in the U.S. on Ukraine's targeting of Russian refineries and said if this deal goes through, it would lower prices for Americans.ELVING: That was supposed to be the idea. It was supposed to do something about these escalating fuel prices, which actually have been with us back to March with the beginning of President Trump's war on Iran. This was supposed to do something about it, but market experts say it can't do much to lower prices in the near term. And as you pointed out, there is no energy ceasefire.So what was the Russia diesel deal really all about? Why was it worth being seen as aiding the Russian invaders of Ukraine, worth being yoked with Vladimir Putin as a dictator seeking his own enrichment? Was it worth signing that executive order, abandoning the Lindsey Graham Act, a bipartisan set of sanctions on Russia that was intended to make Iran want to negotiate? All these things together seem to indicate a clear shift away from backing Ukraine to backing Putin and Russia in this, their latest aggression and land grab.SIMON: As midterm elections loom, the U.S. Department of Justice is suing the state of California to block the counting of ballots from people the government says are, quote, "likely noncitizens." What do we know about this case?ELVING: Trump is renewing his long-running assault on voting in California. He said when he lost the state in 2016, that there were millions of people voting illegally. He offered no proof, no evidence, just assertion. And here we are a decade later, and he's still saying essentially the same thing. He has his Department of Justice making these claims elsewhere too. But when the thumb drives arrive full of names and then they are checked, they don't prove illegal voting.We should note that the conservative Heritage Foundation maintains a database of all sorts of voter violation cases, and over the last 40 years, it's found 99 cases of ineligible alien voters nationwide. And a Fox News poll this past week showed people care about voter fraud but did not rank it among their most important concerns.SIMON: That's the economy, right?ELVING: Oh, the economy - that's the underlying message here. Higher prices for fuel help raise prices on a host of things, and they kick off another cycle of escalating inflation. So high prices across the board and an unpopular trade war with Canada and a still more unpopular war on Iran, and now corruption coming up to top the list for many voters.SIMON: Finally, President Trump this week reversed the decision made by Secretary of Defense Hegseth to livestream the execution of the convicted Fort Hood shooter. Do we know what prompted that change?ELVING: You know, it might just have been a dose of good sense or a sudden realization that the world would see a full firing squad opening fire on a man who's been in a wheelchair for years. So when first asked about this, the president said he backed Hegseth and the public execution, absolutely. But was the president fully informed of the content of this spectacle and the likely fallout or the unintended consequences? And if not, do we have an example or a metaphor here for how things have happened?In so many other ways in the administration, poorly prepped decisions, poorly prepared personnel of the kind of vetting of qualifications that we saw in the matter of the sad story of Trump's latest press secretary, Katie Zacharia. It turns out not had not passed the bar. It's a set of questions worth asking and waiting to have answered to.SIMON: NPR's Ron Elving. Thanks so much.ELVING: Thank you, Scott.

title: Politics chat: Zelenskyy on Trump, Democrats bring in the money for midterms
description: From Russia to AI to Iran, President Trump has taken political stances that put him at odds with much of the electorate.
body:
From Russia to AI to Iran, President Trump has taken political stances that put him at odds with much of the electorate.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  President Trump says the White House was not behind the recent throttling of satellite internet services to Ukraine. Elon Musk, whose company provides the service Ukraine relies on for battlefield operations, points out it's owned and operated by the U.S. government. That's where we'll start today with NPR senior national political correspondent Mara Liasson. Good morning, Mara.MARA LIASSON, BYLINE: Good morning.RASCOE: Ukraine called it a deliberate move, and it also decried some U.S. sanctions on Russia that have been waived, right? Tell me about that.LIASSON: That's right. President Trump has taken a number of steps recently that critics say would help Russia, not Ukraine, in Russia's efforts to subjugate Ukraine. He signed that executive order on Friday that lift tough new sanctions on Russia. Those are from the Lindsey Graham bill, which the president had just signed, and it was about to go into effect. A few days before that, he said the U.S. would start buying Russian diesel fuel. That potentially violates the law Congress passed in 2022, barring the U.S. from importing Russian gas without congressional approval.And as for that suspension of the Starlink-Starshield satellite system that Ukraine uses to help intercept Russian missiles, access to that is controlled by the U.S. military, and the president is the commander in chief. Trump has also demanded that Ukrainian leader Zelenskyy be replaced. He declared an energy ceasefire that Russia immediately violated with no consequences. And he's also shown in the past a real affinity for Russian leader Vladimir Putin and a real animus against Ukrainian leader Zelenskyy. But he's never taken so many steps all at once that would help Russia.RASCOE: NPR's Joanna Kakissis just sat down with Zelenskyy, and he was really outspoken. Here he is on himself versus President Trump.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)PRESIDENT/NPR CLIP VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: We are different people. I think that President Trump, maybe he likes such people like Putin.RASCOE: Is that the motivation here? The politics don't seem very cut-and-dry.LIASSON: No. But part of the politics is that Trump has been making efforts - so far unsuccessful - to get the price of gas and diesel down before the midterm elections, even though oil experts say whatever diesel Russia could sell is really not enough to bring prices down very much. But he did get pushback from members of Congress for these latest moves in favor of Russia - mostly Democrats, but a few Republicans. But according to polls, the war in Ukraine in itself is not a top issue for voters this fall.RASCOE: I mean, but this fall, as you're talking about, what is happening with the landscape? The midterms are coming up fast.LIASSON: That's right. This week, we saw some eye-popping fundraising numbers that could reflect a big enthusiasm gap that favors Democrats. According to the latest campaign finance filings, individual Democratic candidates are bringing in tons of money. They're outraising their Republican opponents in key Senate races like Texas and Alaska and Ohio, Maine, Michigan, Iowa. The Republican campaign committees and super PACs have been vastly outspending their Democratic equivalents. Elon Musk, for instance, has donated more than $150 million to help the Republican candidate Ken Paxton in Texas.But Paxton's Democratic opponent James Talarico has raised six times as much as Paxton this quarter, and those kinds of individual donations, usually in smaller denominations, they are a pretty good proxy for enthusiasm and another sign that Democrats are on offense and Republicans are on defense, especially in red states.You know, another sign of this is Donald Trump's travel schedule. This week, he's going to North Carolina, Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa. He's already been to Alaska and Texas and Georgia. These are red states that, in the past, Republicans should have been able or would have been able to take for granted.RASCOE: Yeah. And so Georgia on Friday - and Georgia's where you most recently had a focus group of swing voters. What did they say?LIASSON: Yes. These are all swing voters. They voted for Biden in 2020, Trump in '24. The biggest takeaway from this week's focus group in Georgia, where Republicans have already pulled out of the Senate race, by the way, and the Democratic candidate looks like he's going to cruise to victory. The biggest takeaway is that even though voters have been sour on Trump all cycle, they really haven't connected their feelings about him to how they're going to vote. But this week, our voters in Georgia, all of a sudden, are talking very strategically about their vote. They say they want their vote to be a check on Trump. They would - say they would be more likely to vote for a candidate who is not going to be a rubber stamp for the president.RASCOE: That's NPR's Mara Liasson. Thank you so much for joining us.LIASSON: You're welcome.

title: With an ad aimed at Trump, this Republican exposed GOP angst about Latino voters
description: Rep. María Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., looks
body:
Rep. María Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., looks on during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on May 20, 2026. Salazar has warned that President Trump's immigration policies could be driving Latino voters away from the GOP.
                
                    Heather Diehl/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Heather Diehl/Getty Images
    

   
   MIAMI – At the heart of Little Havana neighborhood here, is Máximo Gómez Park, also known as Domino Park. Cuban Americans play games of dominos here to escape the pressures of daily life.   But what started as a typical day at the park last week took a turn: Miami police arrested a player in the middle of a game after a dispute with a city worker. It spurred other players to worry about deportations, setting off a broader political debate over whether President Trump or former President Biden was responsible for a higher cost of living.   
   "It's Biden," said Alejandro Torres, a Republican voter.   "It's Trump," responded Ricardo Carracedo, who plans to vote for Democrats in the midterm elections.   
   This same divide is playing out across Florida's 27th Congressional District, a Miami-Dade County seat that is more than 70% Latino. It is a warning for Republicans, whose 2024 wins relied heavily on this crucial electorate.   That year, Trump cut Democrats' margin with Latino voters nationally to just three points – down from 25 points four years earlier, according to Pew Research Center. Cuban Americans, the district's largest Latino group, have been reliable Trump supporters. But many of their friends and relatives have been swept up by the administration's deportation agenda. A crack among them could signal broader trouble for Latino support for Republican candidates.   Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Cuban-American Republican in her third term, has been sounding the alarm. Last month, Salazar filmed a television ad in front of the White House warning President Trump that he's "gone too far" on immigration.   "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," she said.   
   Trump hit back at Salazar after the ad. On his TruthSocial account, he shared a post in which another user called her a "back stabber."   Salazar told NPR she didn't see the comments as attacks, saying she later spoke to the president.   "I told him, 'You know, what I'm telling you is what my people are feeling,'" she said. "This is Democracy where we tell the boss, 'hey, this is what's happening in my neck of the woods.' And that's exactly what I did."   
   Salazar's read of the effect of Trump's policies may be right. Polling firm Equis Research found in a recent survey of registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino that if the election for Congress were held today, voters would pick the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a margin of 57 to 31.   At a Salazar campaign event this past Thursday, friends Mirla Loredo and Ramona Tunon were divided on whether they sided with her take or Trump's.   "Him, I tell you," Loredo said in Spanish.   "I like her position," Tunon said.   Salazar has pushed against aggressive immigration policies in the past. For several years, she has proposed legislation she called the Dignity Act to block deportations of immigrants considered pillars of their community – such as hospitality, construction and farm workers.   
   Still, Carracedo, the Democratic voter from Domino Park, said he'll vote a straight blue ticket. He said Salazar's recent push against Trump's aggressive deportations is too little, too late.   "I'm not going to vote for her, because at the last hour she's defending Hispanics. But the entire time she supported Trump and the money Trump wanted for ICE," or Immigration and Customs Enforcement, he said in his native Spanish.   Trump, he said, reminds him of the communist leaders he left behind in Cuba.   In the past, Republicans' messaging on socialism had a powerful impact on this district. But now that message has lost some of its potency, eclipsed by worries about a higher cost of living and deportations.   Eduardo Gamarra, a politics professor at Florida International University, says the local economy's malaise has eclipsed all other issues.   "It's probably the number one thing. And that cuts across all of the electorate," he said.   He said the second top issue is deportations, which have devastated some Miami businesses that have lost workers and customers.   
   An opening for Democrats   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Florida Democratic Congressional candidate Eliott Rodriguez campaign at the CAO Bakery and Cafe on Oct.16, 2026 in Miami. Rodriguez, like Salazar is a former broadcast journalist with Cuban roots.
                
                    Joe Raedle/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Joe Raedle/Getty Images
    

   
   Salazar's Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, is a former broadcast journalist with Cuban roots like Salazar. He says he wants to revamp the immigration judge system, and restore federal food assistance after cuts that have hurt constituents.   Still, he concedes his party has a lot of ground to make up after largely walking away from Florida.   "One of the biggest mistakes that Democrats have made in Florida is to think that Florida is unwinnable. But I beg to differ."   Polls in the district have shifted more towards Democrats' direction in recent weeks, but Republicans are still favored. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated the race "lean Republican."   Gamarra, the politics professor, says the GOP will need to rely on its political infrastructure to pull out a win   "They're not going to win on the issues ... They're going to win on turnout … the enthusiasm is on the Democrat side. But Republicans have a machinery."

title: What role does the White House Press Secretary play in the Trump era?
description: NPR's Ayesha Rascoe asks Adm. John Kirby, who had spokesperson roles in the Obama and Biden administrations, about the utility of the role of t
body:
NPR's Ayesha Rascoe asks Adm. John Kirby, who had spokesperson roles in the Obama and Biden administrations, about the utility of the role of the White House Press Secretary.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  This week may bring a new White House press secretary. Or maybe not. Katie Zacharia left the role after less than a week. She posted on social media on Friday night that it had been an honor to work for President Trump. This came after questions about her credentials. She called herself a lawyer, but hadn't passed the bar exam. And she had an unsteady performance in her first and only briefing.John Kirby was a familiar face behind the podium of the White House briefing room. He was there in the later days of the Biden administration. He was a spokesperson at the Pentagon before that and was a rear admiral in the Navy. John Kirby is now director of the University of Chicago's Institute of Politics, and he joins us now. Admiral, welcome.JOHN KIRBY: Thank you so much, Ayesha. Good to be with you today.RASCOE: I want to talk less about Katie Zacharia's tenure, which was extremely short, and more about the actual job of a White House press secretary. Like, who does the press secretary really answer to? Does the press secretary answer to the public or to the president?KIRBY: Well, ultimately to both, but from an inside-the-lifelines perspective, it's clearly to the president. You are expected to be the president's voice and sometimes the president's face on issues on a daily basis, which means you have to have access to the president. You have to know what the president's thinking about, whatever the policy issue is. But you also are accountable to the American people. Your job as a spokesperson is to be honest with them, to tell them as much as you can, as quickly as you can, and be as forthright in answering tough questions from the press as possible.The other thing that's important to remember is the benefit of holding your policies up to the scrutiny of an independent press, a press that is not afraid to challenge you and the president and the administration on those policies. That actually helps inform, or should help inform, the policymaking process for the American people.RASCOE: Can you talk about how this administration's approach - do you think it's permanently changed the press secretary's role?KIRBY: I don't believe that they have eliminated or permanently changed what the role of the press secretary is. And look, you have to give them credit where it's due. They continue to hold near-daily briefings at the White House. Now, the information that's being shared isn't always honest or truthful, but they are out there every day. And obviously, the president still values the role of a press secretary or he wouldn't have worked so diligently and so quickly to find a replacement for Karoline Leavitt.What they have changed, though, is the makeup of the press corps and the way the press corps is treated and respected. You know, they favor right-wing outlets almost exclusively, and they have shunned - literally and figuratively - qualified independent media outlets like Politico and CNN and MS NOW simply because they don't like the coverage. So those are dangerous practices that are indefensible, but I don't believe that the practice of having a White House press secretary has fundamentally changed. The way they do it absolutely has changed, and I'd like to see those changes reversed at some point, but I believe they still value the role.RASCOE: Should there be something more formal regulating the role of a press secretary, like legislation? Because right now, it's mainly guided by custom, right?KIRBY: That's right. I mean, every president decides who their press secretary is. The press secretary is not Senate-confirmed. It's a individual staff decision. But no, I don't believe it should be legislated. I don't believe that it should be regulated. I think the tradition has survived this long for a reason.RASCOE: Before I was hosting on Sundays and with the, you know, puzzlemaster Will Shortz, I was a White House correspondent in the briefing room. And what I found was, as you said, like, the press secretary not only delivers the message, but they have to be able to explain the message. And that requires answering follow-ups, actually engaging in questions. The problem with that is that it can be combative. In some ways, it has devolved into kind of sniping back and forth (laughter). And how do you have the substantive debate without devolving into attacks?KIRBY: It is the job of the press secretary to maintain composure and to not let that heated atmosphere become, as you put it, contentious. That is hard to do in this current environment right now, but I believe it's absolutely vital. You're not friends. They have a job. You have a job.RASCOE: Well, can I ask you, though, because whether it's issues about a president's health, which have gone through multiple administrations, or whether it's national security issues - right? - there are questions of not just do you trust the press, but do you trust an administration, right? How can a White House press secretary restore trust to the American people?KIRBY: When I was at the podium, I always thought about my mom. Now, she's going to be turning 90 years old here in December. She follows the news. She's whip-smart. And so whenever I was answering a question in the briefing room, I tried to think about her and how can I answer this question, how can I respond to this issue in ways that she'll understand, that she'll grasp? And let me tell you something. If she didn't, I would hear about it. I'd get a text right after a briefing or an interview, and she would tell me, like, you know, I don't understand what you're talking about there. So, like, she was a good litmus test for me.And I think just basic, simple use of language and talking the way you would with your folks back home and your friends. And then the last thing is constantly being available - available to the public, available to the press. It's a contact sport. You got to physically be on the field to play. And I think that's really important, too.RASCOE: That's John Kirby. He served in the Obama and Biden administrations as well as at the U.S. Navy. He's now director of the University of Chicago Institute of Politics. Admiral, thank you so much for speaking with us.KIRBY: My pleasure. Thank you.

body:
Katie Zacharia is out as press secretary, White House says   Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role as press secretary, according to a White House official not authorized to speak on the record, marking a stunning turn of events for the spokeswoman.

    
        Politics
    


                  
            October 16, 20264:29 PM ET
         
      

      
      Katie Zacharia is out as press secretary, White House says 
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6005302/nx-s1-9967568" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    




      Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role as press secretary, according to a White House official not authorized to speak on the record, marking a stunning turn of events for the spokeswoman.   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  From NPR News, this is ALL THINGS CONSIDERED. I'm Ailsa Chang.SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  And I'm Scott Detrow. It was over almost before it began. The White House's newest press secretary is out after just five days on the job. Katie Zacharia started her job at the beginning of the week. She gave her first and only press briefing on Tuesday. The briefing was noticeably short and widely panned, and then questions emerged about her legal credentials. NPR's Emily Feng has been following Zacharia's rapid rise and rapid fall and joins us now in the studio. Welcome.EMILY FENG, BYLINE: Hi, Scott.DETROW: Let's start with this. What has President Trump said about what is happening with Zacharia's job?FENG: So Trump was asked earlier today about this. He strongly hinted that she was leaving, but he said he was giving her the option to decide if she wanted to resign.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I said, Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want. She said, this is a lot tougher. I said, welcome to the world of Trump.FENG: And a senior White House official told NPR she is, quote, "transitioning out" of this very, very new job. Trump noted that she'd had a really rough time with how the media was treating her, and so he asked her if she still wanted to do this job.DETROW: Let's talk more about this because a big part of the reason why she has faced so much scrutiny this week was this possible misrepresentation of her legal credentials. Can you explain what happened?FENG: Yeah, so Trump has referred to her as an attorney, and Zacharia did go to law school. But there is no record of her passing the bar in any state. And when she was asked about this, she responded that she had passed when she moved to China. Now, Scott, you know, I've lived in China for the better part of a decade. It is just not possible for foreigners to take the bar there or even practice law. Zacharia later said she misheard the question about when she passed the bar, and then she defended herself last night on Fox News when questioned by Sean Hannity about her professional record.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)KATIE ZACHARIA: I graduated Pepperdine, got married in the same week, and we had all intent to move out to China. I sat for it because I didn't want to have a withdraw status.DETROW: So if Zacharia is out after a week, that leaves the White House once again without a press secretary. How much of an issue is that?FENG: According to Trump, it's no problem. He has shown he is very comfortable with the idea of mostly speaking for himself, regardless of whether that's good or bad for the Republican Party. There - it's been almost two months, I should note, since Karoline Leavitt, the last press secretary, left. And so there have not been regular press briefings for months now. And Trump frequently comes out and just directly takes questions from reporters at the White House, sometimes with very little notice.And so Trump, it looks like, will continue to be his own spokesperson, but this is a really critical juncture for him right now. His approval ratings as president are at the lowest for his presidency. And yet, he's in full throttle for midterm campaigning. You know, he's hitting the road again today. He's in Georgia. He just spoke at a rally this afternoon. And he's hoping to defy polling that shows Republican candidates are really back on their heels right now in this midterm election.DETROW: That is NPR's Emily Feng. Thank you so much.FENG: Thank you, Scott.

title: Trump promised a swing district blitz. He's going to a lot of very red states
description: President Trump speaks at a campaign ral
body:
President Trump speaks at a campaign rally at Laughlin/Bullhead International Airport in Bullhead City, Ariz., on Oct. 14.
                
                    Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   📲Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App      Early in September, President Trump gathered Republicans running in competitive races for a dinner in the White House Rose Garden. Prime aged beef burgers were on the menu as the president made a pledge to spend the final month before the midterms campaigning for the approximately 30 Republican candidates in attendance.   "I'm going to go to every one of those 35 places and we're going to see if we can get everyone elected," Trump said confidently.   The White House hasn't clarified which 35 places the president was talking about that night. Since then, Trump has campaigned with fewer than a third of those candidates. Rather than focus on swing states and swing districts as the president said he would, his travel schedule has taken him to a lot of Republican territory.   
   Trump's itinerary is both a reflection of where he can help (and where he can't) but also of a shifting landscape where even red state Republicans need a boost.   
   On the tarmac between rally stops in Arizona and Montana this week, Trump attempted to spin his visits to states he won decisively just two years ago as a matter of gratitude.   "So, I do it to thank them," Trump said. "I also do it because we have some great people there that are running and I want to make sure they win."   He went on to bemoan the drop in Republican turnout in years when he isn't on the ballot, something Trump and his team are trying to counteract with an October campaign rally blitz that has taken him to Ohio (twice), Texas (twice), Oklahoma and even Tennessee.   "What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?" Trump mused from stage to wild cheers.   Earlier this week, the president took an eight hour flight to Alaska to campaign for Republicans, Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Rep. Nick Begich, both of whom face races that are too close for comfort in a state Trump won by 13 points in 2024.   "This is worth the 8 hours in a plane," Trump said to an adoring crowd. "And don't forget I've got 8 hours going back. Give me credit for that."   
   In fact, he made two more stops on the way back and spent the night at the Trump hotel in Las Vegas.   The Republican National Committee has announced he'll be campaigning in Kansas Monday, which has a toss-up U.S. Senate race, something few would have anticipated even a month ago.   
   Republicans are on defense in a lot of states where they've traditionally won without much trouble. Trump's team is picking locations where he can activate the Republican base in places where he's done well in the past.   "Just a lot of excitement, a lot of momentum building up on the ground here," said RNC Chairman Joe Gruters in a call with NPR from a Trump rally in Arizona. "It's turnout, turnout, turnout. How do you get the base to show up? You put the president on the ballot. You put him out there."   Trump frequently implores his supporters to vote as if he were on the ballot. It's a novel political strategy that runs counter to the norm for unpopular presidents whose parties face significant midterm headwinds. Trump claims the polls are wrong about his underwater approval rating.   As for Trump's message, it doesn't change much from stop to stop. There are the greatest hits: his past election wins, his One Big Beautiful Bill, and a walk down memory lane from right before he launched the war with Iran when gas prices were cheaper. He teases a $5,000 dividend to every American adult if Republicans win the House and the Senate, an idea he first rolled out at the unconventional Republican midterm convention, but has faced resistance from elected Republicans. On most stops he talks about a specific project or deal he has planned for the state.   On Tuesday, Trump is set to campaign in Greenville, North Carolina. Republican campaign committees have already started canceling ad reservations meant to help Trump's handpicked Republican Senate candidate there, Michael Whatley. It's a sign they see that race as moving out of reach.   
   There's also a congressional district in Eastern North Carolina that was redrawn to favor Republicans as part of Trump's mid-decade redistricting push. It shouldn't be competitive, but it's now rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report.   "I think it's going to backfire on them this year in every way shape and form," said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. "He's trying to drum up any amount of support that he can at the last minute. But I don't think that North Carolinians are going to fall for it again."

title: Fraud, affordability and Trump policies drive friction in Minnesota Senate debate
description: The major party candidates for Minnesota's U.S. Senate seat faced off in an hourlong debate Friday on MPR News with fraud, affordability and fa
body:
The major party candidates for Minnesota's U.S. Senate seat faced off in an hourlong debate Friday on MPR News with fraud, affordability and fallout from the Trump administration's policies as key points of friction.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  Tight Senate races in Texas, Iowa and Kansas are getting a lot of attention during this year's midterm elections. But Minnesota also has a close race, and Peter Cox from Minnesota Public Radio joins us now. Thanks so much for being with us.PETER COX, BYLINE: Good morning, Scott.SIMON: Please tell us who's running and why this race has maybe been a little overlooked nationally.COX: So Peggy Flanagan, a progressive Democrat who's been lieutenant governor in Minnesota for the last eight years, is up against Republican Michele Tafoya, who spent years as a sideline reporter for Monday Night Football and Sunday Night Football. And they're battling for a seat that's been held by Democrats since 2009. Recent polls have shown the two neck and neck, though Flanagan had a 4% edge in the most recent one.But normally, such a tight margin would mean political parties would be pouring money into this race. But that's not what's happening here. This election, Republicans are facing challenges in what would be reliably red states, so they've been putting their money into shoring up those races instead. And that seems to be a big reason why Minnesota's race has been much quieter, even though it's one of several that could determine which party controls the U.S. Senate.SIMON: President Trump indicated this week he might make a trip to Minnesota. How big a factor has President Trump been in this race?COX: Yeah. Like many of these midterm races we're seeing nationwide, President Trump is a major factor. Tafoya, who has never held public office before, said when she announced her candidacy she'd be honored to have his endorsement. But in recent months, she's tried to distance herself from Trump. And that became tougher this week when Trump was speaking at a campaign rally in Ohio, and he railed against members of Minnesota's Somali community who he said were looting Minnesota welfare programs. He then implored people to get out and vote for Tafoya.During a debate yesterday, Tafoya was asked whether she'd campaign with Trump if he comes to Minnesota, and she didn't answer the question. Peggy Flanagan has consistently said Tafoya would be a lapdog for Trump and was quick to point out how Tafoya only recently has tried to distance herself from the president in this campaign.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PEGGY FLANAGAN: Minnesotans are smarter than this new version of Michele Tafoya who has shown up in the final weeks of this campaign. Give me a break.SIMON: Governor Tim Walz's administration has gotten a lot of heat over the fraud that you mentioned. Has this extended to Lieutenant Governor Flanagan, who, after all, is his second in command?COX: Yes. About 70 people have been convicted of bilking millions of dollars from state programs in the last few years, and questions have been raised about why the Walz administration didn't respond more quickly. During the debate, Tafoya was quick to point the finger at Flanagan.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MICHELE TAFOYA: This historic fraud happened under her watch, and suddenly, she's looking out for Medicaid and SNAP? Sell it to someone else, Peggy.COX: Now, Flanagan says the issue was not under her purview as lieutenant governor.SIMON: The Trump administration cited this fraud as one reason for the increased immigration crackdowns in Minnesota last winter. Is that enforcement surge playing a role in this race?COX: Well, the monthlong surge has been eclipsed recently by other issues like the economy and cost of living, but it's definitely still resonating. And Flanagan has commended the large-scale protests against ICE in Minnesota and has called for the agency to be dismantled. Now, Tafoya has criticized the rollout of the enforcement surge and called the fatal shootings of Americans Renee Good and Alex Pretti by immigration agents devastating. But she also criticized the protests and said local leaders encouraged them.SIMON: Peter, any signs this race might get a last-minute influx of outside spending, as we've seen elsewhere?COX: Well, the president talking about this race this week, saying he might visit, could put it more front and center for some. But we haven't seen any big changes in political spending here in the last few days. About two weeks ago, U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune came to stump for Tafoya at a farm in Southern Minnesota. And when he was asked whether the political action committee he helps run - the Senate Leadership Fund - would give Tafoya a funding boost, he was noncommittal. And we still haven't seen much national money flowing in to support either candidate. We're a little more than two weeks out from the election, so the runway for that kind of investment in this race is getting pretty short.SIMON: Peter Cox of Minnesota Public Radio. Thanks so much for being with us.COX: You're welcome.(SOUNDBITE OF CHROMEO SONG, "CABIN FEVER")
